title: British Mother Referred to Prevent Counter-Extremism Programme After Trip to Israel
excerpt: Holly Passmore, 44, learned from police records she obtained months later that an anonymous referral said she had "over-identified" with the Israel-Palestine conflict. Durham Constabulary took no further action.
body:
• Holly Passmore, 44, a mother of two from County Durham, was visited at home by two plain-clothes police officers after an anonymous referral to Prevent, the UK government's counter-extremism programme.
  • Police records she later obtained said the referral claimed she had "over-identified with the conflict between Israel and Palestine" and was "supportive of Israel to the point that she has travelled to Israel".
  • Durham Constabulary took no further action against her; she says a senior officer later acknowledged the force had got it wrong.
  • Prevent referrals reached a record 8,778 in the year to March 2025. Ministers describe the programme as voluntary safeguarding; rights groups say it chills lawful political expression.

A British mother of two was visited at home by police investigating an anonymous referral to Prevent, the UK government's counter-extremism programme, after the referral said she had "over-identified" with Israel and had travelled there in support of the country. Holly Passmore, 44, from County Durham, learned the reason only months later, when she obtained her police file through a subject access request. The case, reported this week by The Telegraph and The Jewish Chronicle, has renewed debate over where Prevent's thresholds sit.

A knock at the door

The visit came at about 11am on 4 July last year. Passmore, who cares for her nine-year-old son, who has severe autism, while studying for a master's degree, assumed the two plain-clothes Durham Constabulary officers were concerned she had taken her son into a war zone on her recent trip to Israel. She told them he had not travelled – he had stayed in England with her mother and her 20-year-old daughter. One of the officers corrected her.

"No, this is about you – because you may be at risk of manipulation."

— Police officer, as recalled by Holly Passmore to The Telegraph

Passmore, a social media influencer who had recently returned from a press trip to Israel, according to The Jewish Chronicle, said the officers told her the visit was a safeguarding matter: they were following up an anonymous referral to Prevent. She suspected her public support for Israel had prompted it, but had no confirmation of who had referred her, or why.

What the referral said

Confirmation came months later, when Passmore used data protection law to obtain the records police held on her. A police intelligence report seen by The Telegraph states that the referral said she "over-identified with the conflict between Israel and Palestine" and was "supportive of Israel to the point that she has travelled to Israel". The report also described her as having "MH" – mental health – issues and being "vulnerable to negative influence".

Durham Constabulary took no further action against her. Passmore has said that a superintendent later visited her home and acknowledged that the force had got things wrong.

How Prevent works

Prevent is the strand of the UK's counter-terrorism strategy, CONTEST, that deals with people before any crime is committed. Anyone – a teacher, a health worker, a member of the public – can raise a concern about someone believed susceptible to radicalisation. Police screen and assess every referral. Most are closed with no further action or passed to mainstream services such as health or social care. Where police assess a genuine risk, the case can go to a Channel panel, chaired by the local authority, which decides whether to offer a tailored support package. That support is voluntary: participation is confidential and requires the person's consent, and a case is closed to Channel if consent is not given.

The programme is handling record volumes. According to Home Office statistics, 8,778 referrals were made in the year ending March 2025, up 27 percent on the year before and the highest total since records began in 2015. Only 17 percent were adopted as Channel cases. Where a type of concern was recorded, the largest category – 56 percent of referrals – involved no identified ideology; extreme right-wing concerns accounted for 21 percent and Islamist extremism for 10 percent.

Safeguarding or overreach?

The government defends Prevent as early intervention, not punishment. In a written statement to Parliament, Security Minister Dan Jarvis said Prevent "aims to stop people from becoming terrorists or supporting terrorism", has supported nearly 6,000 people "to move away from a pathway to radicalisation" since 2015, and "plays a vital role in safeguarding those most vulnerable in our communities". He said it must remain "threat agnostic", intervening before an ideology has clearly taken hold; the Home Office issued new guidance in September 2025 clarifying referral thresholds.

Critics argue that a low referral threshold carries its own harms. Amnesty International UK has said Prevent has a "chilling effect on the lives and freedoms of thousands of innocent people", with individuals modifying their behaviour and refraining from expressing religious and political views. Campaigners at Prevent Watch argue that even a referral that goes no further can leave personal data retained across police databases. In Passmore's case, the referral produced a home visit and a police file, but no finding of wrongdoing.

What happens next

Passmore has chosen to speak publicly about the referral. There is no suggestion of any criminal investigation, and the identity of the person who referred her remains unknown – Prevent referrals can be made anonymously. The case is likely to feature in the continuing scrutiny of Prevent by the Independent Prevent Commissioner, a post created in December 2024 to oversee the programme.
nri_angle: The referral of a pro-Israel British mother to Prevent has become a flashpoint in the UK debate over counter-extremism thresholds and free expression, watched closely by Jewish and diaspora communities in Britain.
